people.name: Scott Santens
people.niche: Universal basic income advocate and writer; former editor of Basic Income Today
people.reason: He argues that automation should free people from jobs and that unconditional income lets people do meaningful unpaid work, separating purpose from paid employment.
people.gap: The map has few voices saying outright that purpose does not depend on paid work; he is the best-known US UBI advocate making that case.

people.name: James Livingston
people.niche: Historian, Rutgers University; author of 'No More Work: Why Full Employment Is a Bad Idea'
people.reason: His Aeon essay argues the belief that a job gives meaning, purpose and character is no longer plausible and asks what people would do if income didn't depend on work.
people.gap: Supplies an explicit post-work rejection of the idea that paid work is the source of dignity and purpose.

people.name: Oren Cass
people.niche: Founder of American Compass; former Manhattan Institute fellow; pro-worker conservative economics
people.reason: He argues a universal basic income should be rejected on principle because it would make work optional and render self-reliance moot, favouring wage subsidies instead.
people.gap: Gives the 'reject' side of guaranteed income a leading pro-work conservative policy voice, alongside Hawley and Vance's camp.

people.name: Robert Shiller
people.niche: Nobel-laureate economist (Yale); behavioral finance, inequality and risk-sharing
people.reason: In his own Project Syndicate column he argues that modest, even temporary, robot taxes should not be ruled out and could fund wage insurance for workers displaced by automation.
people.gap: Adds a mainstream economist who supports taxing labor-replacing automation, a side currently carried only by two progressive politicians.

people.name: Lawrence Summers
people.niche: Former US Treasury Secretary, Harvard economist; growth-first centrist
people.reason: In his own op-ed he calls a tax on job-replacing robots illogical, 'protectionism against progress', and prefers growing the pie then redistributing through taxes, transfers and retraining.
people.gap: Adds the best-known mainstream economist rejecting a special tax on labor-replacing automation.

people.name: Mark A. Lemley
people.niche: Stanford law professor; leading US copyright and IP scholar
people.reason: His co-authored article 'Fair Learning' is the most-cited academic argument that AI training on copyrighted works should generally be permitted.
people.gap: Gives creators-owed-for-training a legal-scholar voice on the reject side.
people.flag: Work is co-authored with Bryan Casey (an academic paper, not a co-signed letter).

people.name: Jeff Jarvis
people.niche: Journalism professor and media critic (BuzzMachine; testified to the US Senate on AI and journalism, Jan 2024)
people.reason: A journalist who argues that AI reading and learning from text is fair use and warns that restricting training sets would harm public discourse.
people.gap: A media-side voice who rejects payment-for-training, unlike most publishers.

people.name: Chris Callison-Burch
people.niche: UPenn computer science professor; testified to the House Judiciary IP subcommittee on generative AI (May 2023)
people.reason: His House testimony explicitly advocates keeping fair use for AI training, warning that per-work licensing would hand AI to incumbents.
people.gap: A technical researcher's voice on the reject side.
people.flag: Lower public profile than most map figures.

people.name: Daniel Jeffries
people.niche: Open-source AI advocate and writer (Future History newsletter; former Stability AI CIO)
people.reason: Argues training on scraped data is fair use and that individual compensation for creators is unworkable and would entrench big companies.
people.gap: An open-source, anti-copyright-expansion voice on the reject side.
people.flag: Modest public profile; former Stability AI executive, so he has an interest in the outcome.

people.name: Bruce Schneier
people.niche: Security technologist and Harvard Kennedy School lecturer; public-interest technology and AI-and-democracy writer
people.reason: He argues for a government-funded and government-directed 'public option' for AI so that development is not left only to private companies.
people.gap: Without him the public-ai-infrastructure statement has almost no explicit proponents of publicly built AI models on the map.
people.flag: Co-authored essay (with Nathan E. Sanders), published under both names; not a co-signed letter, but check the rule.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: Basic Income, Not Basic Jobs: Against Hijacking Utopia

statements.where: reply to Sarris: 'Getting a sense of purpose from your job is a crapshoot at best. Getting a sense of purpose outside your job is a natural part of the human condition'; retirees example
opening ('I've pushed for a basic income guarantee before') and closing ('Basic income is a real shot at utopia')

works.note: Not AI-specific: argues UBI over a jobs guarantee in general, with a nod to future em/superchild disadvantage. Page includes a long comment thread; the passages cited are in the post body, before 'This entry was posted'.

works.author: scott-santens
works.title: Why We Should All Have a Basic Income

statements.where: whole essay; automation section on mechanistic work handed off to machines
'the difference between doing meaningless work for money, and using money to do meaningful work'; unpaid caregiving and open-source work

works.note: The dignity reading is moderate: he says purpose comes from intrinsically motivated (often unpaid) work, not that people need no work at all.

works.author: james-livingston
works.title: What if jobs are not the solution but the problem? (Fuck work)

statements.where: opening: belief that 'a job gives meaning, purpose and structure' is 'no longer plausible... ridiculous'; later 'a world in which the job no longer builds our character'

works.note: Pre-dates generative AI; framed around automation and insufficient work. Publication date from memory of Aeon listing; confirm. Does not explicitly propose UBI in the text I scanned, so not tagged for income-not-tied-to-work.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Why Universal Basic Income Is a Bad Idea

statements.where: 'UBI is a flawed idea, not least because it would be prohibitively expensive'; close: 'dribble out enough crumbs to keep people at home, distracted, and otherwise pacified'

works.note: Original at project-syndicate.org is paywalled; Daily Maverick carries the full syndicated text with Project Syndicate copyright line. Framed explicitly around automation and globalization. He concedes UBI beats mass impoverishment and prefers a negative income tax / expanded EITC.

works.author: oren-cass
works.title: Why a Universal Basic Income Is a Terrible Idea

statements.where: early: 'even if it could work, it should be rejected on principle... It would make work optional and render self-reliance moot'

works.note: Not AI-specific; responds to automation-motivated UBI proposals (Andy Stern, Robert Reich, Charles Murray). Also implies work gives dignity (hold side of work-gives-dignity) but not tagged.

works.author: robert-shiller
works.title: Taxing The Robots?
works.channel: Social Europe (syndicated Project Syndicate column, 'Robotization Without Taxation?')

statements.where: closing paragraphs: 'let's not rule out so quickly at least modest robot taxes' and 'A moderate tax on robots ... seems a natural component of a policy to address rising inequality'

works.note: Author's own syndicated column (Project Syndicate original is paywalled; this full-text reprint carries the PS copyright line). Stance is hedged: modest/temporary robot tax, revenue to wage insurance. About robots/automation generally, written 2017, not AI specifically.

works.author: lawrence-summers
works.title: Robots are wealth creators and taxing them is illogical
works.channel: larrysummers.com (repost of his op-ed; site dates it to Washington Post March 5, 2017)

statements.where: opening rebuttal of Bill Gates's robot-tax proposal; 'Mr Gates' robot tax risks essentially being protectionism against progress'

works.note: Direct reply to Gates's 2017 robot-tax interview. Concerns robots/automation broadly, not AI by name; argues for retraining and transfers instead. Site headline says Washington Post but the text matches his FT column of the same title; date is the column date.

works.author: gavin-newsom
works.title: Veto message: Senate Bill 7 (No Robo Bosses Act)
works.channel: Office of the Governor of California

statements.where: paragraphs 3-4: bill 'imposes unfocused notification requirements' and 'overly broad restrictions on how employers may use ADS tools'

works.note: WEAK. Scanned image PDF (no text layer; readable only by OCR/vision). Bill-specific veto: he says 'I share the author's concern' that unregulated employer use of automated decision systems can harm workers and defers to forthcoming CPPA rules. He rejects this law's worker-notice and limits, not the principle of worker say. Readers may well code it neutral.

works.author: mark-lemley
works.title: Fair Learning (with Bryan Casey)
works.channel: Texas Law Review 99:743 (draft PDF hosted by Berkeley Law)

statements.where: Introduction: 'we argue that ML systems should generally be able to use databases for training, whether or not the contents of that database are copyrighted'

works.note: PDF is the 2020 pre-publication draft; text extracts with pdftotext. Argues for permitting training under fair use; it does not explicitly address payment schemes beyond saying copyright claims would stop the use without compensating anyone in particular.

works.author: jeff-jarvis
works.title: Copyright and AI and journalism
works.channel: BuzzMachine (his blog; his comment to the US Copyright Office AI inquiry)

statements.where: 'As for Question 8 on fair use ... hard to see how reading and learning from text and images to produce transformative works would not be fair use'

works.note: He also warns that restricting training sets to free content would leave AI built on misinformation. A related post, buzzmachine.com/2024/01/09/journalism-and-ai/ (his Senate testimony text), says he was 'delighted' his books were in Books3.

works.author: chris-callison-burch
works.title: Testimony before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, IP and the Internet: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property

statements.where: Opening list item 3: 'Advocacy to retain fair use for the purposes of training AI systems'; later: requiring 'an explicit license from the copyright holder' would jeopardize progress

works.note: 15 MB PDF with a text layer. He acknowledges that many artists disagree, and he favors opt-out tools, but his stated position is to retain fair use rather than require licensing.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: Synthetic Data in AI: Implications for Policy

statements.where: 'The Main Idea' section: copyright 'theft' framing attributed to 'AI cynics and opponents'; restricting copyrighted data 'not a meaningful barrier'; 'Model training is rather unambiguously a form of speech'

works.note: WEAK/INDIRECT: he never says outright that companies should not pay. He dismisses the theft framing and data-restriction bills and treats training as protected speech. Readers may code this as unclear.

works.author: daniel-jeffries
works.title: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion

statements.where: 'Scraping that data was absolutely fair use'; 'Anyone thinking that artists, writers, coders, and content creators are going to get compensated individually is out of their mind'

works.note: Explicit. Part of his argument is that compensation is unworkable, but he also argues normatively against expanding copyright to cover training.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: The Case for Public AI Infrastructure

statements.where: intro list of 'things government should build' and the section 'The Case for Public AI Research Infrastructure'

works.note: Moderate hold. He backs publicly accessible AI research infrastructure (compute and data for academics) built by the federal government, and prefers a federal effort to California's CalCompute. This is research infrastructure, not government-run consumer AI systems, so readers may grade it as a partial hold.

works.author: bruce-schneier
works.title: Build AI by the People, for the People

statements.where: 'It's time to start taking AI development out of the exclusive hands of private companies' and the 'public option' paragraphs

works.note: Strong, explicit hold: calls for 'a government-funded and -directed AI program to develop widely reusable models in the public interest'. Co-authored with Nathan E. Sanders.

works.author: gary-marcus
works.title: What Could Possibly Go Wrong with Sam Altman's New Ambitions?

statements.where: closing paragraphs: 'Even if the $7 trillion bet succeeded ... it might tear apart society through radically increased unemployment and social inequality'

works.note: Weak-to-moderate reject. He treats AI-driven social inequality as a harm even in the success case, but he does not directly address the 'everyone ends up better off' condition.
